Text: Java source files use the {{c1::.java}} extension, while compiled bytecode files use the {{c2::.class}} extension.
Extra: Source is human-written; bytecode is executed by the JVM.

Text: {{c1::JVM}} stands for Java Virtual Machine.
Extra: The JVM executes bytecode and manages runtime behavior.

Text: {{c1::JRE}} stands for Java Runtime Environment.
Extra: The JRE provides the JVM and runtime libraries.

Text: {{c1::JDK}} stands for Java Development Kit.
Extra: The JDK includes development tools such as `javac`.

Text: {{c1::JVM}} runs bytecode, {{c2::JRE}} runs Java applications, and {{c3::JDK}} builds Java applications.
Extra: This is the short memory rule.

Text: The Java compiler command is {{c1::javac}}, while the command used to run a compiled class is {{c2::java}}.
Extra: Compile first, run second.

Text: `javac HelloWorld.java` produces {{c1::HelloWorld.class}} if compilation succeeds.
Extra: The output is bytecode.

Text: A `.class` file contains {{c1::bytecode}}, not human-friendly Java source code.
Extra: Bytecode is the JVM instruction format.

Text: Java has two basic execution phases: {{c1::compile time}} and {{c2::runtime}}.
Extra: Compile time checks/translates; runtime executes.

Text: At runtime, the JVM can load classes, verify bytecode, execute instructions, manage memory, and perform {{c1::JIT compilation}}.
Extra: JIT is runtime optimization.

Text: JIT stands for {{c1::Just-In-Time}}.
Extra: JIT can compile hot bytecode into native machine code.

Text: Garbage Collection reclaims memory from objects that are no longer {{c1::reachable}}.
Extra: Reachability is more precise than "not used anymore".

Text: Setting a reference variable to {{c1::null}} may make the old object eligible for Garbage Collection if no other references remain.
Extra: It does not force immediate collection.

Text: Java is called platform independent because compiled {{c1::bytecode}} can run on different platforms with compatible {{c2::JVMs}}.
Extra: The JVM itself is platform-specific.

Text: The JVM itself is built for a specific {{c1::operating system}} and {{c2::CPU architecture}}.
Extra: Bytecode is portable; JVM implementations are platform-specific.

Text: Java robustness is helped by strong static typing, exception handling, automatic memory management, array bounds checking, and no normal {{c1::pointer arithmetic}}.
Extra: This list explains why Java avoids some dangerous low-level errors.

Text: Java supports {{c1::multithreading}}, meaning multiple threads of execution can run inside one process.
Extra: Useful for servers and background tasks.

Text: Multithreading can introduce problems such as {{c1::race conditions}} and {{c2::deadlocks}}.
Extra: Concurrency is powerful but risky.

Text: Java SE means {{c1::Java Standard Edition}}.
Extra: Java Core mostly means Java SE fundamentals.

Text: Jakarta EE was formerly called {{c1::Java EE}}.
Extra: Older resources may still use the Java EE name.

Text: Java ME means {{c1::Java Micro Edition}}.
Extra: It was designed for smaller or embedded devices.

Text: Java 8 introduced lambda expressions, functional interfaces, Stream API, and the new {{c1::Date and Time API}}.
Extra: These features remain important in modern Java code.

Text: LTS stands for {{c1::Long-Term Support}}.
Extra: Java 11, 17, and 21 are commonly discussed LTS releases.

Text: Java 21 is known for modern features such as {{c1::virtual threads}}.
Extra: Virtual threads matter for scalable concurrent server applications.

Text: For learning Java Core today, {{c1::Java 17}} or {{c2::Java 21}} is a good default.
Extra: Still recognize Java 8 features for legacy projects and interviews.

Text: {{c1::Bytecode}} is the intermediate instruction format stored in `.class` files and executed by the JVM.
Extra: It is not source code and not native machine code.

Text: {{c1::Runtime}} is the phase when a compiled program is actually executing.
Extra: Runtime errors happen during execution.

Text: {{c1::Class loading}} is the JVM process of finding and loading class definitions needed by a running Java program.
Extra: Class loading is not object creation.

Text: {{c1::Reachability}} describes whether an object can still be accessed through active references from the running program.
Extra: Garbage Collection depends on reachability.

Text: Before Java, C/C++ compiled code directly to host-specific {{c1::native machine code}}, causing a compile-per-platform problem.
Extra: Java solved this by compiling to bytecode run on the JVM.

Text: Every compiled Java `.class` file begins with the 4-byte hexadecimal magic number {{c1::0xCAFEBABE}}.
Extra: The JVM classloader checks this magic number to verify that the file is a valid compiled class.

Text: At the storage level, Java source code is stored as {{c1::plain text}} (usually UTF-8), whereas bytecode is a structured {{c2::binary format}}.
Extra: Bytecode contains version metadata, a constant pool, and JVM stack opcodes.

Text: The Java Garbage Collector only reclaims memory allocated on the {{c1::Heap}}, not primitives or reference variables allocated on the {{c2::Stack}}.
Extra: Stack frames are automatically deallocated when a method exits.

Text: Java GC identifies garbage by starting from {{c1::GC Roots}} and performing {{c2::reachability analysis}}.
Extra: Any Heap object with no reference path back to active GC Roots is deemed unreachable and eligible for reclamation.

Text: Designated Java versions like Java 8, 11, 17, and 21 are called {{c1::LTS}} (Long-Term Support) versions, which receive years of active updates.
Extra: Non-LTS versions are only supported for 6 months.

Text: Java 21 introduced Project Loom's {{c1::virtual threads}}, which drastically improve server concurrency by decoupling Java threads from OS threads.
Extra: This allows millions of concurrent tasks to run on minimal hardware resources.
